## The two NIEs on Iran, and the fatwa

On *National Security Files* in July 2026, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) said the community-wide assessment of the Iran nuclear question is not a close call: two separate National Intelligence Estimates — one in 2003, one *"like 2009, something like that"* — concluded on the coordinated agreement of all eighteen U.S. intelligence agencies that Iran did not have a nuclear-weapons programme.<Cite t="01:02" /><Cite t="01:32" /> Kiriakou pairs the NIEs with a fatwa from Ayatollah Khamenei declaring the development of a nuclear weapon a sin — the doctrinal reason, on his account, that Iran had not enriched to weapons-grade levels.<Cite t="02:03" /> Kiriakou dates the modern *"six months from a nuclear weapon"* Israeli talking-point on Iran to 1986 and treats it as a claim continuously falsified for forty years.<Cite t="00:30" />

## The 1997 NIE coordinated in eight hours

On *National Security Files* in July 2026, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) said the piece of paper that promoted him to GS-14 was a National Intelligence Estimate he wrote in 1997 titled *"Iraq: Saddam's Next 12 Months."* The estimate went through the eighteen-agency coordination process in eight hours — a speed the presiding National Intelligence Officer, Ben Bonk, told him was *"the fastest coordination session for an NIE that I've seen in 25 years."* Kiriakou attributes the speed to a modest premise no agency could plausibly reject: *"[Saddam](/wiki/saddam-hussein) could threaten Kuwait, Saddam could threaten the Kurds, Saddam could threaten the Shiites, Saddam will probably try to violate sanctions. Big deal."*<Cite t="02:03" /><Cite t="02:34" /><Cite t="03:05" />

## The Bush-era 'policy recommendation' paragraph

Just before he left the [CIA](/wiki/cia), [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) says, George W. Bush ordered a controversial edit to the format of the President's Daily Brief. The one-page lead article and the paragraph-of-fact-plus-paragraph-of-analysis structure of the shorter articles were left intact, but Bush added a third paragraph headed *"policy recommendation."* Kiriakou reads the addition as an inversion of the agency's constitutional posture: *"that flies in the face of everything that the CIA is — you're supposed to be the one that makes the policy, not the CIA. The CIA can tell you what the facts are and what the facts likely mean, but then you make a decision."* The recommendation paragraph, on Kiriakou's telling, survived only through Bush's second term.<Cite t="05:42" /><Cite t="06:13" /><Cite t="06:44" />

## Uncle Bill of Steubenville

On *National Security Files* in July 2026, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) told a family story he learned only in his mid-teens. His maternal great-uncle Bill had come home from Dachau — one of the American soldiers who liberated the concentration camp — with what modern medicine calls PTSD. In 1953, Kiriakou says, Bill *"somehow got it into his head that Richard Nixon, who had just been elected vice president, promised him a job at the post office in Steubenville, Ohio."* Bill put on a suit that Monday morning and went to the post office to claim the job; when told no such promise existed he answered *"that damn Nixon, I'm going to get him."* Six months later Nixon came to Steubenville to give a speech; Bill tried to enter the civic centre with a .45. He was disarmed and arrested. Kiriakou records his mother's summary of the near-miss: *"there but for the grace of God, our name could have been Oswald."* Bill later died being struck by a train under circumstances his mother told him were *"one of those things that's better just left unresolved."*<Cite t="25:52" /><Cite t="26:23" /><Cite t="26:55" /><Cite t="27:27" /><Cite t="27:57" />

donald-trump.body_append:
## 'I just go with my gut'

On *National Security Files* in July 2026, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) contrasted [Donald Trump](/wiki/donald-trump)'s stated method with that of every prior modern American president. Asked on 60 Minutes *"who are your closest advisers?"*, Trump had answered — as Kiriakou paraphrases the exchange — *"I don't have any. I just go with my gut."* Kiriakou treats this as a discontinuity from a longstanding norm under which *"any other president will ask the Secretary of State, 'what do you think?' Secretary of Defense, 'what do you think?' National Security Adviser, 'what do you think?' CIA director, 'what do you think?'"* on major policy decisions.<Cite t="05:42" /><Cite t="06:44" />
